NB3 FW
Process		Ecological Mire Restoration—Re-bogification of exhausted peat extraction fields
7
Restoration
Implementation
Methods		Restoring the water regime to the natural one
8
Partial closure of the ditch network using peat-made dams (turbast paisudega)
9
Filling the dicthes with the soil in the embankments
10
Construction of overflow thresholds (ülevoolupaisud) — 25 units with geotextile reinforcement, controlling maximum water levels per zone
11
Construction of Type 1 small peat dams — 250 units on internal ~1 m-wide field drains
12
Construction of Type 2 and 3 large peat dams — 43 units on larger drains (1–4 m wide)
13
Tree felling for machine access tracks (trassiraie ~3.6 ha) and to create open-water and open-mire conditions (0.7 ha + 2.4 ha)
14
Planting of cranberry (harilik jõhvikas, Vaccinium oxycoccos) cuttings on ~0.3 ha — replacing part of former blueberry plantation
15
Construction of citizen science trail (harrastusteaduse rada) with bridge (purre) over main drainage ditch and QR-code information posts
16
Creation of new ~100 m ditch section in northern part to prevent water regime changes on adjacent private lands
17
DriversPressureImpact
Inferred from: Restoration plan for Kõrsa mire (https://media.voog.com/0000/0050/7864/files/RestPlan%20K%C3%B5rsa%2004.12.2023_EE.pdf )
18
Extensive drainage of the peatland★★★★★
82.1 km total drainage network; 70.9 km of small (~1 m wide) internal field drains; active drainage since 1966
19
Historical peat extraction★★★★★
Large-scale extraction 1966–1998 (Pärnu EPT then AS Torfex/Jiffy Products Estonia); current E-class peat field status (Helm et al. 2020)
20
Habitat destruction/bare peat surface★★★★☆
Spontaneous revegetation very slow even 20–30 years post-abandonment; invasive Campylopus introflexus carpets bare peat and blocks bog species recovery
21
Biodiversity loss★★★★☆
Original bog ecosystem destroyed; remaining rare species present only at margins and along tracks; most area below minimum threshold for Natura 2000 classification
22
Increased GHG emissions★★★★★
Bare drained peat emitting 1–4 t C/ha/yr; net CO₂ source; carbon balance modelling confirms ongoing atmospheric impact (Kull, TÜ)
23
Adjacent active peat mining (AS Jiffy Products Estonia)★★★☆☆
Mining area 74.18 ha immediately south; license L.MK.PM-13269 until 2049; expansion application for additional 174.39 ha; EIA underway (OÜ Inseneribüroo Steiger)
24
ATV damage and fire risk★★★☆☆
ATV ruts documented across area; dry bare peat = high fire risk; ATV activity documented as potential ignition source; culverts used as ATV crossings removed during restoration

briefly describe the expected benefits from the NB3 process on the habitats of the Restoration UnitBriefly explain data, monitoring, knowledgeLink to resourcesSelect Level
66
• Habitat type classification of Natura habitats cannot be applied due to significant alteration of peatlands due to intensive peat mining.
• Habitats based on vegetation with current and target status: Open transitional mire from 1ha to 61.40ha, Semi-openbog from 18.7ha to 33.10ha, Bog forest from 18.1ha to 26.40ha, Transitional mire forest from 0ha to 66.80ha, Mire habitats from 116.8ha to 207ha.
• Current dominant vegetation classes (mapped 2022): rabamännik (bog pine woodland), kõdusoomets (peat decay forest), lageraba (open bog), puhmaraba (dwarf-shrub bog), puis-puhmaraba (forested dwarf-shrub bog), siirdesoo kohati õõtsikuga (transitional mire with quagmire), rikutud kuid taastumisvõimeline raba (disturbed but restorable bog), erineval määral taimestunud jääksoo (variously vegetated residual bog), tiigid (fire-pond pools), vähese taimestikuga teeäärised ribad (road-edge strips).
• Short-term (3–5 years post-restoration): Sphagnum moss cover increases in wetter areas; bare peat colonised by bog-characteristic species; Campylopus introflexus carpet retreats; water bodies at open areas increase lakeshore and reed communities; cranberry spreads from planting areas.
• Long-term (>30 years): Area converges toward natural transitional mire or raised bog; self-regulating hydrological regime re-established; Kõrsa bog connectivity improved — restoration area becomes contiguous buffer for the intact Kõrsa bog to the east. 77
Flora (8 protected species found 2022, all LNC Category II–III):
* Leucobryum glaucum (LK II — white cushion moss, most sensitive); Lycopodiella inundata (harilik sookold, LK III); Lycopodium calvatum (karukold, LK III — found in multiple locations); Orchis militaris (hall käpp, LK III — multiple individuals); Platanthera bifolia (kaheleheline käokeel, LK III); Listera ovata (suur käopõll, LK III); Dactylorhiza maculata (kuradi-sõrmkäpp, LK III — very few); Dactylorhiza fuchsii (vööthuul-sõrmkäpp, LK III — very few); Sphagnum wulfianum (Wulfi turbasammal, LK III — very few).
* None previously registered in EELIS for this location
* 2022 finds submitted to EELIS during project.
* Restoration expected to improve conditions for all, as none grow in zones where water table will rise to surface level.
Fauna — Birds:
* From EELIS and PlutoF records, protected species found on restoration area: Tetrao tetrix (teder/black grouse — found in 2022 survey); Grus grus (sookurg/common crane); Dryocopus martius (musträhk/black woodpecker).
* From adjacent Kõrsa bog: Tetrao urogallus (metsis/capercaillie) — critical population, Kõrsa bog is connector between Soomaa-Kikepera core zone and Luitemaa population.
* Dunlin: Calidris alpina schinzii (niidurüdi) — LK I category.
* Kõrsa dunlin permanent habitat established January 2023, overlapping restoration area eastern zone—breeding site known since 2007.
* Also from adjacent bog: Haliaeetus albicilla (merikotkas/white-tailed eagle), Circus pygargus (soo-loorkull), Limosa limosa (mustsaba-vigle), Numenius arquata (suurkoovitaja), Pluvialis apricaria (rüüt) — all priority wader species.
Fauna — Dragonflies (2022 inventory, 19 species):
* Protected species found: Leucorrhinia pectoralis (suur-rabakiil, EU Habitats Directive Annex II & IV) — 2 males found; Leucorrhinia albifrons (valgelaup-rabakiil) recorded from adjacent Kõrsa bog.
* Common species include Agonum ericeti (raba-ketasjooksik — indicator of natural bog quality) found on 3/5 transects = 60 individuals.
Fauna — Amphibians (2022):
* Pelophylax lessonae (tiigkonn/pool frog) in fire ponds.
* Rana temporaria (rohukonn/common frog) in shallow wet areas.
* Both under nature protection in Estonia.
* Moor frog (rabakonn, Rana arvalis) recorded from earlier data.
Fauna — Beetles (30 species, pit traps):
* Notable: Agonum ericeti (raba-ketasjooksik/bog disc-runner — key indicator) — 60 individuals on 3/5 transects, confirming residual bog quality
* Dolomedes fimbriatus (hiidämblik/great raft spider — indicator of wetland quality). This is significantly better than Lavassaare where this indicator was absent.		Restoration plan for Kõrsa, Section 2.4, 2.5, and Annex IIRestoration plan for Kõrsa:
